shortExplanation: The two additions contribute $6$ before the doubling.
detailedSteps: If the original numbers are $u,v$, their new sum is $2(u+3)+2(v+3)=2(u+v)+12=2S+12$.
commonMistakes: Adding 3 just once to the total.
difficultyNotes: The operation is applied separately to both entries.

shortExplanation: The tens digit cancels because it is nonzero.
detailedSteps: Write the number as $10a+b$, with $a\ne0$. The condition is $10a+b=ab+a+b$, so $9a=ab$. Division by $a$ gives $b=9$.
commonMistakes: Allowing a zero tens digit.
difficultyNotes: The digit restriction justifies cancellation.

shortExplanation: The $p$-dependent terms cancel from the tax equation.
detailedSteps: The effective rate is above $p$, so the income $I$ exceeds $28000$. In percentage-scaled units, the tax equation is $28000p+(I-28000)(p+2)=I(p+0.25)$.
Canceling $pI$ gives $2I-56000=I/4$, so $(7/4)I=56000$ and $I=32000$.
commonMistakes: Applying the higher rate to the entire income.
difficultyNotes: Separate the bracket amount from the excess income.

shortExplanation: Express the extremes in terms of the mean.
detailedSteps: Let the mean be $m$. The least and greatest entries are $m-10$ and $m+15$, while the middle entry is $5$.
Their sum must be $3m$, so $(m-10)+5+(m+15)=3m$. Thus $m=10$ and the total is $30$. The entries $0,5,25$ have the required order.
commonMistakes: Treating the median as the mean.
difficultyNotes: Checking the order confirms the algebraic solution is allowed.

shortExplanation: Divide the factorial by the product of its even factors.
detailedSteps: The product $10000!$ includes every desired odd factor and all even factors $2,4,\ldots,10000$.
The even-factor product is $2^{5000}(1\cdot2\cdots5000)=2^{5000}5000!$. Dividing removes exactly the even factors.
keyIdeas: Separating even factors from a factorial
commonMistakes: Dividing by 5000! without removing the 5000 factors of 2.
difficultyNotes: The endpoint 10000 belongs to the even factors.

shortExplanation: Only the blocks $642$ and $9753$ leave three digits summing to $9$.
detailedSteps: The decreasing even block can be $864,642,$ or $420$. The decreasing four-odd block can be $9753$ or $7531$.
The sums of the three unused digits for these six pairings are respectively $3,11,9,17,15,23$. Only $642$ with $9753$ leaves $8,1,0$, giving the first block $810$ and $A=8$.
commonMistakes: Treating zero as forbidden in all positions.
difficultyNotes: Distinctness makes the complementary digits determined.

shortExplanation: The full price must be the integer divisor $23$.
detailedSteps: Let $p$ be the full price and $F$ the number of full-price tickets. Doubling the revenue gives $p(140+F)=4002$.
There must be $0\le F\le140$, so $4002/280\le p\le4002/140$. The only integer divisor of $4002=2\cdot3\cdot23\cdot29$ in this interval is $23$.
Then $140+F=174$, so $F=34$. Full-price revenue is $34\cdot23=782$.
keyIdeas: A divisor constraint from ticket revenue
commonMistakes: Assuming the half price must itself be a whole number of dollars.
difficultyNotes: Use the full-price integer condition after eliminating the half-price count.

shortExplanation: The sector radius becomes the slant height and its arc becomes the base circumference.
detailedSteps: The arc length is $(252/360)(2\pi\cdot10)=14\pi$, so the base radius is $7$.
The slant height remains $10$, rather than the vertical height. The source diagram with slant height $10$ and base radius $7$ is choice C.
keyIdeas: Rolling a circular sector into a cone
commonMistakes: Reading the sector radius as the vertical height.
difficultyNotes: Inspect the location of each dimension label in the answer diagrams.

shortExplanation: Use the input ratio $600/500=6/5$.
commonMistakes: Multiplying the value by the input ratio.
difficultyNotes: One direct substitution avoids unnecessary reconstruction of the whole function.

shortExplanation: Pentagons occupy $5/9$ of a $3$-by-$3$ repeating patch.
detailedSteps: Scale each illustrated square to side $1$. A period of the pattern has area $9$ and contains four unit-square tiles.
The rest of that patch belongs to the pentagons, so their area fraction is $(9-4)/9=5/9$. This is about $55.56\%$, closest to $56\%$.
keyIdeas: Area of a repeating tiling patch
commonMistakes: Counting tiles instead of adding their areas.
difficultyNotes: Different tile shapes need not have equal area.

shortExplanation: White finishes first exactly when the final chip in a full random order is red.
detailedSteps: Imagine drawing all five chips, even after the stopping time. The last white appears before the last red precisely when the final chip of this full order is red.
In that case both whites have already been drawn while at least one red remains, so the actual last drawn chip is white. The final chip is red with probability $3/5$.
keyIdeas: Completing one color in a random order
commonMistakes: Equating the answer with the probability the first chip is white.
difficultyNotes: A full permutation gives a simpler description of the stopping event.

shortExplanation: Count multiples of $3$ or $4$, then remove those divisible by $5$.
detailedSteps: The first count is $\lfloor2001/3\rfloor+\lfloor2001/4\rfloor-\lfloor2001/12\rfloor=667+500-166=1001$.
Among these, multiples of $5$ are multiples of $15$ or $20$, totaling $133+100-33=200$. Subtraction gives $801$.
commonMistakes: Subtracting every multiple of 5, including numbers outside the first union.
difficultyNotes: Apply inclusion–exclusion separately to the excluded part.

shortExplanation: The two function values at any common input sum to $2k$.
detailedSteps: Reflection sends $y$ to $2k-y$, so the two quadratic expressions sum identically to $2k$.
Setting $x=1$ in this sum yields $a+b+c+d+e+f=2k$.
commonMistakes: Reflecting about the x-axis rather than y=k.
difficultyNotes: Coefficient sums are function values at 1.

shortExplanation: Pair-based construction counts each all-polygon triangle three times.
detailedSteps: Each of the $\binom92=36$ pairs supports two equilateral triangles in the plane, for $72$ pair-and-side constructions.
Exactly three equilateral triangles have all three vertices among the polygon vertices: their index sets are $\{1,4,7\}$, $\{2,5,8\}$ and $\{3,6,9\}$. Each was counted three times instead of once.
Subtract $2$ extra counts per such triangle: $72-2(3)=66$.
commonMistakes: Counting only equilateral triangles whose three vertices belong to the polygon.
difficultyNotes: The requirement is at least two polygon vertices.

shortExplanation: Two neighboring faces unfold to a rhombus with endpoint distance $1$.
detailedSteps: Call the opposite edges $AB$ and $CD$. Unfold faces $ABC$ and $BCD$ across $BC$. With $B=(0,0),C=(1,0)$, their third vertices are $A=(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$ and $D=(1/2,-\sqrt3/2)$. The two midpoints become $(1/4,\sqrt3/4)$ and $(3/4,-\sqrt3/4)$, distance $1$. The joining segment crosses $BC$, so this length is attainable.

For the lower bound, a shortest path need not enter any face twice: the part between two visits could be replaced by a straight segment in that convex face. Thus it crosses a chain of two, three or four distinct faces.

Unfolding those finite chains gives endpoint distances $1$ for every two-face and three-face chain; the four-face chains give either $1$ or $\sqrt3$. Each path length is at least its unfolded endpoint distance. Therefore no path is shorter than $1$.
commonMistakes: Using the spatial straight-line distance, which passes through the tetrahedron.
difficultyNotes: An attainable unfolded segment and a lower bound both establish shortest length.

shortExplanation: Each sock/shoe pair removes half of all labeled orders.
detailedSteps: There are $16!$ orders of the sixteen distinct items. For each leg, swapping the positions of its sock and shoe reverses that pair’s order.
The eight pair swaps partition all orders into classes of size $2^8$, containing exactly one order with every sock before its corresponding shoe. Hence the count is $16!/2^8$.
commonMistakes: Putting all socks on before any shoe, which unnecessarily restricts the order.
difficultyNotes: The eight precedence constraints act on distinct pairs.

shortExplanation: The favorable region is the semicircle on diameter $AB$ lying inside the pentagon.
detailedSteps: Thales’ theorem identifies the disk on diameter $AB$ as the locus of obtuse $\angle APB$. Here $AB^2=4^2+(-2)^2=20$, so that disk has radius $\sqrt5$.
The pentagon lies on one side of $AB$, and its other four sides contain the entire semicircle on that side. Thus the favorable area is $\pi(\sqrt5)^2/2=5\pi/2$.
The pentagon area is $4(2\pi+1)-(1/2)(4)(2)=8\pi$. The probability is $(5\pi/2)/(8\pi)=5/16$.
keyIdeas: An obtuse-angle locus inside a polygon
commonMistakes: Using the entire disk, including the half outside the pentagon.
difficultyNotes: The locus must be intersected with the sampling region.

shortExplanation: Horizontal separations are twice the geometric means of the radii.
detailedSteps: For two tangent circles of radii $u,v$ resting on the same line, the horizontal center separation $h$ satisfies $h^2=(u+v)^2-(u-v)^2=4uv$.

The centers of the radius-$1$ and radius-$4$ circles are horizontally $4$ apart. The middle radius-$r$ circle contributes separations $2\sqrt r$ and $4\sqrt r$, giving $6\sqrt r=4$. Therefore $r=4/9$.
keyIdeas: Circle tangency above a common line
commonMistakes: Using center-to-center distances as horizontal separations.
difficultyNotes: The source figure selects the circle in the gap between the others.

shortExplanation: The constant coefficient fixes the common value as $-2$.
detailedSteps: The y-intercept gives $c=2$, so the product of the three roots is $-c=-2$. Their mean is $-a/3$, hence $a=6$.
The coefficient sum is $1+a+b+c=-2$, giving $1+6+b+2=-2$ and $b=-11$.
commonMistakes: Using c rather than -c for the product of cubic roots.
difficultyNotes: Keep the sign in the cubic product formula.

shortExplanation: The original diagonals must be perpendicular and have equal length.
detailedSteps: The midpoint quadrilateral has adjacent sides parallel to $AC$ and $BD$, with half their lengths. It is a square precisely when these diagonal vectors are perpendicular and equally long.

Here $AC=(2,-6)$. A perpendicular equal-length vector is $(6,2)$ or $(-6,-2)$. Starting at $B=(1,1)$ yields $D=(7,3)$ or $(-5,-1)$. Only $(7,3)$ is in the first quadrant, so the coordinate sum is $10$.
commonMistakes: Requiring the original quadrilateral itself to be a square.
difficultyNotes: The first-quadrant condition chooses the allowed diagonal direction.

shortExplanation: The shared shifted factors constrain the variables to a small divisor list.
detailedSteps: Thus $b+1$ is one of $3,7,21$, the divisors above $1$ of $\gcd(525,147)=21$. For $3$, the resulting $c+1=49$ cannot divide $105$. For $7$, the tuple is $(74,6,20,4)$, whose product is $35520$, not $8!$.
For $21$, the tuple is $(24,20,6,14)$, with product $40320=8!$. Hence $a-d=24-14=10$.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract 1 from the shifted factors.
difficultyNotes: The product condition distinguishes the remaining integral candidates.

shortExplanation: Scale to a unit rectangle and find the two intersections.
detailedSteps: The lines $EF$ and $EG$ have equations $y=6x-2$ and $y=-6x+4$. Their intersections with $AC$ are $H=(2/5,2/5)$ and $J=(4/7,4/7)$.
The determinant formula gives $[EHJ]=3/70$ in the unit rectangle. Area ratios are unchanged by this scaling, so the actual area is $70(3/70)=3$.
commonMistakes: Assuming H and J divide the diagonal into equal thirds.
difficultyNotes: Separate the shape-independent area ratio from the stated total area.

shortExplanation: The non-real pair must have integral sum and integral product.
detailedSteps: Dividing the monic integer polynomial by its two monic integer-root factors leaves a monic quadratic with integer coefficients. Its non-real roots are conjugates.
For $\alpha=(1+i\sqrt{11})/2$, the pair has sum $1$ and product $3$, so its quadratic is $x^2-x+3$. For example, $x(x-1)(x^2-x+3)$ supplies a valid quartic with two real integer roots.
The other proposed conjugate pairs have products $1/2,5/4,5/4,7/2$, respectively, so they cannot be the roots of the required integer quadratic.
commonMistakes: Testing only the real part while ignoring the conjugate product.
difficultyNotes: Monic division by integer linear factors preserves integer coefficients.

shortExplanation: Normalize $BD=1$, giving $BC=3$, then use the $15$-degree angle.
detailedSteps: Put $B=(0,0),D=(1,0),C=(3,0)$ and $A=(t,t)$ with $t>0$, because the angle at $B$ is $45^\circ$. The dot product for vectors $AB=(-t,-t)$ and $AD=(1-t,-t)$ is $2t^2-t$. Since their angle is $15^\circ$, it is positive.
The cross-product magnitude is $t$, so $\tan15^\circ=1/(2t-1)=2-\sqrt3$. Thus $t=(3+\sqrt3)/2$.
At $C$, $\tan\angle ACB=t/(3-t)=2+\sqrt3=\tan75^\circ$. The angle is acute because $t<3$, giving $75^\circ$.
commonMistakes: Selecting an obtuse branch when using a tangent equation.
difficultyNotes: The signs of the dot products determine the correct angle branches.

shortExplanation: Every sequence repeats after five terms, so four distinct equations suffice.
detailedSteps: The neighbor relation rearranges as $a_{n+1}=(a_n+1)/a_{n-1}$. Starting with $x,2000$ gives the cycle $x,2000,2001/x,(x+2001)/(2000x),(x+1)/2000,x,2000,\ldots$. All these terms are positive for $x>0$.
The second position cannot equal $2001$. The other four positions give respectively $x=2001$, $x=1$, $x=2001/4001999$, and $x=4001999$.
These four positive values are distinct and exhaust the cycle, so the answer is $4$.
commonMistakes: Generating only the first three terms or failing to prove periodicity.
difficultyNotes: Positivity ensures every division is valid and the cycle persists.
